claims.text: The initial material is an as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy containing dual-phase B2/fcc lamellar colonies.
The as-cast lamellar colonies are prone to microcracking during room-temperature tensile loading.
The intervention consists of multi-step forging at approximately 600–700 °C with controlled incremental strain.
The forging is followed immediately by a short-duration sub-solvus anneal of approximately 30–60 minutes.
Moderate-temperature multi-step forging will refine the lamellar spacing and reduce lamellar-colony size.
A short sub-solvus anneal will partially recrystallize and stabilize the forged lamellar colonies.
The anneal will relieve residual stress and refine sub-grain boundaries.
The resulting structural mediator is reduced lamellar-colony size with stabilized internal boundaries.
Smaller defects and improved phase-boundary cohesion will suppress microcrack initiation.
Refined colony and lamellar dimensions will facilitate progressive dislocation-slip transfer across interfaces.
Slip transfer and shearing across coherent lamellar boundaries can alleviate local stress concentration rather than create a crack.
The forged-and-annealed alloy will have higher room-temperature yield strength than the unmodified as-cast baseline.
The forged-and-annealed alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile elongation than the unmodified as-cast baseline.
The forged-and-annealed alloy will exhibit lower microcrack density and greater strain to failure than the baseline.
Forging must occur near but below the melting or eutectic temperature to avoid excessive grain growth.
Excessive deformation or annealing may cause coarsening or unexpected phase transformations.
Failure to increase both ultimate tensile strength and tensile elongation, or persistence of prevalent microcracking, would falsify the hypothesis.
